sections.h2: How does selling a house in Mt. Lebanon work?
sections.html:
A Mt. Lebanon sale follows the usual Pennsylvania routes of listing with an agent, selling directly to a buyer, or taking a cash offer, with a few municipal and county steps layered on top. Mt. Lebanon is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, roughly four to six miles south of downtown Pittsburgh, and its Inspection Office, tax office and county records all influence the closing date.

The sections below cover the local pieces a seller should line up first, from open permits to the 2026 tax rates and the county appeal calendar.

sections.h2: What kind of homes do Mt. Lebanon sellers own?
sections.html:
Most Mt. Lebanon houses are early twentieth century commuter homes. The first streetcar line to Pittsburgh opened on July 1, 1901, the Liberty Tubes followed in 1924, and the population jumped from 2,258 in 1920 to 13,403 in 1930, according to Wikipedia. The municipality says 4,400 properties sit inside a National Register historic district established in 2014, with Foursquare, Tudor, Colonial Revival, Bungalow and Dutch Colonial styles all common.

Age shows up when a buyer inspects roofs, windows, porches, masonry and basement drainage. The municipality publishes an illustrated design guide for historic homes and a contractor vetting guide, which helps an owner decide whether to renovate before listing or sell without touching it.

Census QuickFacts puts the 2020 to 2024 typical value of an owned home in Mount Lebanon township at $378,300, with 72.3 percent of units occupied by owners across 13,646 households. Median household income over the same period was $123,771, and 67.9 percent of adults 25 and older have finished a four-year degree.

sections.h2: Which Mt. Lebanon permits and inspections can delay a closing?
sections.html:
Open building permits are the most common local snag, because the Inspection Office states that lien letters will not be issued while permits are open. A seller who finished a deck, remodel, furnace swap or fence should confirm every final inspection is on record before setting a settlement date.

  • Work started without a permit can draw fines set by the magisterial district judge, so ask the Inspection Office how to regularize it.
  • Residential building permits generally issue within 15 business days, while zoning permits for items such as an air conditioning unit, driveway, fence or shed take up to 30 days.
  • Fences in single-family districts may reach six feet in side and rear yards, are not allowed in front yards, and cannot be solid.
  • A front porch may extend no more than 10 feet into the front yard, and new or replaced front stairs need a building permit.
  • Every private swimming pool carries an annual operation permit and a safety inspection.

On the first Wednesday of each month the office holds Inspections Consultations from 2 to 5 p.m. Appointments last 30 minutes and require preregistering at 412-343-3408.

sections.h2: What do Mt. Lebanon owners pay in property tax?
sections.html:
A Mt. Lebanon parcel carried a combined 42.963 mills in 2026, divided among the municipality, the school district and Allegheny County. The municipal tax office, on the ground floor of the municipal building, collects real estate tax for both the municipality and the Mt. Lebanon School District.

2026 real estate millage on a Mt. Lebanon parcel (source: Mt. Lebanon tax office)
Taxing bodyMills
Mt. Lebanon Municipality4.50
Mt. Lebanon School District32.033
Allegheny County6.43
Combined42.963

Hypothetically, a house with a county assessed value of $200,000 would produce about $8,593 a year at that combined rate. Collection runs from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount period through July 31, a face period from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty after that. The school portion can be paid in installments, and unpaid balances move to private delinquent collectors each March.

The tax office can supply a bill or receipt, and a title company will usually ask for one before closing. For address changes, the Allegheny County Treasurer handles the request.

sections.h2: How are Mt. Lebanon assessments set, and when can an owner appeal?
sections.html:
Allegheny County assesses every Mt. Lebanon parcel on a 2012 base year, and the last county-wide reassessment took place in 2013. The county office may change a value only for omissions, mathematical or clerical errors, physical changes such as demolitions or building permits, and the occasional interim request from a school district or municipality.

The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears challenges. The annual window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 through September 1, 2026, and the board mails residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead. It applies a common level ratio to the market value in appeals, and that ratio is 49.3 percent for the 2027 tax year.

A catastrophic loss such as a fire allows a reduction request within six months of the event. Buyers of non-owner-occupied property now face a registry rule too: under Act 29 of 2026, effective September 18, 2026, they must send contact details to the chief assessor within 30 days of purchase, and a false filing can bring a fine up to $500.

sections.h2: What transfer taxes and recording steps apply to a Mt. Lebanon sale?
sections.html:
Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax starts at 1 percent of the value transferred, and Allegheny County adds municipal and school district shares so the total ranges from 2 to 5 percent across the county. The county Department of Real Estate collects both the state and local portions at recording, and the tax goes on a separate check from the recording fees.

The county's own example splits a 2 percent total into 1 percent to the state, half a percent to the township and half a percent to the school district. Ask the Department of Real Estate for the rate list entry covering Mt. Lebanon and its school district, since the local share is set by those bodies.

Some family transfers are exempt, and a Statement of Value (form REV-183) is required when the deed lists no consideration or claims an exemption. The state notes that grantor and grantee are jointly liable, so the settlement statement should show who pays.

sections.h2: Which parts of Mt. Lebanon draw buyers?
sections.html:
Buyers tend to focus on walkable blocks near Uptown, which runs along Washington Road (U.S. Route 19 Truck) and holds 182 businesses and 72 storefronts. Beverly Road forms a second commercial strip on the north side, and the Red Line light rail stops at Mt. Lebanon Station beneath Uptown, running through the Mt. Lebanon Tunnel toward the city.

Named neighborhoods include Virginia Manor, Hoodridge, Mission Hills, Seminole Hills, Beverly Heights and Washington Park. The Mt. Lebanon School District operates seven elementary schools, two middle schools and one high school, and it is a walking district with no school bus service. Fifteen parks cover about 200 acres.

Retail news is also local: on October 29, 2026, the municipality posted that Wegmans will anchor a reimagined Galleria of Mt. Lebanon, with renovations expected to begin in 2028.

sections.h2: When does a cash sale fit a Mt. Lebanon house?
sections.html:
Cash works best when the closing date or the property's shape matters more than a retail price. A cash buyer purchases as is, so repairs and permit clean-up fall into the buyer's own plan. Typical situations include:

  • An inherited house with older systems that no one in the family wants to renovate.
  • A property with unfinished or unpermitted work that would take weeks of Inspection Office review.
  • A tenant-occupied house where the owner wants out of landlord duties.
  • A move on a short timeline, such as a job change that leaves two mortgages.

Whoever buys, ask the Inspection Office whether any permit is open before agreeing on a closing date, since municipal lien letters are part of the paperwork.

faqs.q: Does Mt. Lebanon require a resale inspection before I sell?
faqs.a: The municipality's permit page describes a Certificate of Occupancy for changes of use, enlarged buildings and new construction, and it does not list one for an ordinary resale. It does say lien letters are withheld while permits are open, so close those out first and call the Inspection Office at 412-343-3408 to confirm anything specific to your address.

faqs.q: When are Mt. Lebanon property taxes due?
faqs.a: Real estate tax is collected from June 1 to March 5 of the following year, with a discount through July 31, face value from August 1 through September 30, and a penalty afterward. School district tax can be paid in three installments, due September 30, December 31 and February 28.

faqs.q: What starts an Allegheny County assessment appeal for a Mt. Lebanon home?
faqs.a: File with Allegheny County's Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review during the annual summer window, which ran July 1 through September 1 for tax year 2027. Bring comparable sales or an appraisal, because the board applies the county common level ratio to market value.

faqs.q: What does the realty transfer tax cost on a Mt. Lebanon sale?
faqs.a: The state charges 1 percent and the local municipal and school shares come on top, so the countywide total ranges from 2 to 5 percent. Ask the Allegheny County Department of Real Estate for the figure that applies to Mt. Lebanon and its school district.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Mt. Lebanon house that has unpermitted work?
faqs.a: Yes, but the municipality warns that work done without a permit can lead to fines set by the magisterial district judge. Ask the Inspection Office how to bring the work into compliance, or discuss an as-is sale with a buyer who will take the house in the condition it is in.
